title: Shouldering
summary: Use your own king as a barrier: push the enemy king off the path instead of running straight ahead.
part.between.title: Between the king and the pawn
part.between.summary: The king does not chase the pawn: it stands in the other king's path, on the same file, two ranks below.
part.wall.title: The king as a wall
part.wall.summary: Walk beside the enemy king, file by file, until it is too far away to help.
part.edge.title: To the edge and the corner
part.edge.summary: Push the enemy king to the edge; in the corner, one square shuts both exits and the pawn runs on its own.
part.game.title: Schlage against Ahues, 1921
part.game.summary: On the way to the pawn, the king passes through the square the other king needed: a master game decided by shouldering.
part.away.title: Away from the pawn
part.away.summary: Sometimes the best king move steps away from the pawn you want to take, or puts off the capture.
part.square.title: Shouldering and the square
part.square.summary: One move does two things: it stays in the square of the enemy pawn and shuts the path of the enemy king.
part.summary.title: Summary
part.summary.summary: The defence that also pushes, the three rules of shouldering, and the practical challenge.
step.t_stairs: The black king is far from the pawn, and so is the white one. If the black king reaches the f-pawn, it is a draw. Which king move prevents that?
step.t_stairs.hint1: Trace the black king's shortest path to f2. Which squares does it have to cross?
step.t_stairs.hint2: The path goes through c4, d3 and e2. Your king can stand in front of that path, not behind it.
step.stairs: 1.Kb3! The white king does not run to the pawn, it runs to the black king's path. From b3 it takes c4 away, and the black king has to step sideways. Every step it takes, my king takes the same step, on the same file, two ranks below. This is shouldering: my king pushes the other one like a basketball player with his shoulder, without touching, just taking up the space.
step.stairsDraw: Now the same position with 1...Kc4! and the black king gets in front: 2.f4 Kd5 3.f5 Ke5 4.f6 Kxf6, draw. 1...Kb4 and 1...Ka4 draw as well: any step forward by the black king arrives in time. A single tempo decides who pushes whom; that is why the shoulder has to come at once, on the first move.
step.d_stairs: Watch the white king walk down the stairs together with the black one. Always on its file, always two ranks below.
step.d_stairs.m1: 1.Kb3. I shut c4, the black king's doorway.
step.d_stairs.m2: 1...Kc5. It goes up a rank to try d4.
step.d_stairs.m3: 2.Kc3. Same step: d4 is shut before it gets there.
step.d_stairs.m4: 2...Kd5. Now it wants e4, the next doorway to the pawn.
step.d_stairs.m5: 3.Kd3. I shut e4 and e2; the black king is still on the outside.
step.d_stairs.m7: 4.Ke3. I have reached the pawn's side without ever letting the other king through. From here on it is the key-squares technique: 4...Kf5 5.Kf3 and my king stands in front of the pawn.
step.stairsMove: The same idea, now with the pawn on g2. Walk down the stairs together with the black king.
step.stairsMove.hint: Always stay on the black king's file, two ranks below it, shutting the square it would enter through.
step.stairsMove.done: Yes. 1.Kb3, 2.Kc3, 3.Kd3 and 4.Ke3: each of your moves shut the door of the moment, and the black king never reached the pawn.
step.t_wall: Both sides have an f-pawn. The black king is far away, on b4, but wants to come back and defend f7. How do you keep it away?
step.t_wall.hint1: The black king has to cross the board to reach the kingside. Which file would it pass through?
step.t_wall.hint2: A whole file can become a wall if your king walks along it, always beside the black king.
step.wall: 1.Kd4! My king stops on the d-file and becomes a wall: c3, c4 and c5 are shut. If the black king goes up, 1...Kb5, I go up with it, 2.Kd5; if 2...Kb6, 3.Kd6, and it stays locked on the a- and b-files. When it is far enough, my pawn advances and my king goes to fetch the black pawn. 1.Ke5?, which looks more active, allows 1...Kc5! and the black king gets through along the c-file: draw. Only 1.Kd4 wins.
step.d_wall: Follow the wall going up, d-file against b-file, until it is time for the pawn.
step.d_wall.m1: 1.Kd4. The c-file is forbidden to the black king: c3, c4 and c5 are shut.
step.d_wall.m2: 1...Kb5. It goes up to get around via c6.
step.d_wall.m3: 2.Kd5. I go up with it, and c6 is shut before it gets there.
step.d_wall.m4: 2...Kb6. One more rank: now it wants c7.
step.d_wall.m5: 3.Kd6. I shut c7 and c5; the black king is four files away from the f7-pawn.
step.d_wall.m6: 3...Kb7. Still on the outside: the c-file never opened.
step.d_wall.m7: 4.f4. Time for the pawn: with the black king four files away, it can no longer get back in time, and my king goes to fetch f7 next.
step.wallMove: Take the wall up together with the black king, d-file against b-file.
step.wallMove.hint: Your king stays on the d-file, on the same rank as the black king, shutting the c-file.
step.wallMove.done: Yes. The wall went up with it. After 3...Kb7, 4.f4 and the f7-pawn falls.
step.t_across: Your king wants to go to the queenside and take the a6-pawn, and the black king wants to come back and defend it. How do you get there first?
step.t_across.hint1: If your king runs straight for a6, how many moves does the black king need to get back? Does it arrive in time?
step.t_across.hint2: The black king's road back is the g-file. Your king can shut it without moving away from it.
step.across: Now all the way to the edge. The white king wants to go to the queenside and take the a6-pawn, but if it runs now, the black king runs along and defends: 1.Ke6? Kg5 and it gets back in time, draw. So 1.Kf6! My king walks down the f-file beside the black king and shuts the g-file, its road back to the b-pawn. I go down with it to the bottom corner; only then does the pawn advance and my king cross over.
step.acrossMove: Push the black king down to the bottom corner, walking down with it.
step.acrossMove.hint: Your king walks along the f-file, always on the same rank as the black king, to shut the g-file.
step.acrossMove.done: Perfect. The black king is in the bottom corner and the road is clear. After 5...Kh1, 6.b4! Kh2 7.Ke3 Kg3 8.Kd4 Kf4 9.Kc5 Ke5 10.Kb6 Kd6 11.Kxa6, and the a-pawn falls with the black king far away. If 5...Kh3, 6.b3 and the king comes in along the same road.
step.corner: And in the corner. The black king on a8 only gets out via b8 and b7, and b7 is its own pawn. 1.Kc7! shuts both at once: it can only walk down the a-file, far from the pawn, and the e-pawn runs on its own, with no need for an escort. 1.Kb6? allows 1...Kb8 and it gets out; 1.Kd7? allows 1...b5 and the black pawn runs: a draw either way.
step.d_corner: The black king locked in the corner while the pawn advances. Notice that my king never leaves c7.
step.d_corner.m1: 1.Kc7. b8, b7 and b6 are shut; the black king can only use the a-file.
step.d_corner.m2: 1...Ka7. The king's only square; if 1...b5, 2.e4 runs with no opponent.
step.d_corner.m3: 2.e4. The pawn runs and the black king cannot even come closer: b8 and b7 are still shut.
step.d_corner.m4: 2...Ka6. It gets out at the side, but too late: the pawn is four squares from queening.
step.d_corner.m5: 3.e5. One more step; the black king has not even entered the pawn's square.
step.d_corner.m6: 3...Kb5. It steps onto the edge of the square, but it is my move.
step.d_corner.m7: 4.e6. The square moves along, and the black king is left outside: 4...Kc5 5.e7 and the pawn queens next move.
step.cornerMove: Lock the black king in the corner with a single move and let the pawn run.
step.cornerMove.hint: The square that shuts b8 and b7 at once.
step.cornerMove.done: Yes. Locked on the a-file, the black king watched the pawn go by.
step.t_schlage: Berlin, 1921. Willi Schlage, with White, against Carl Ahues. The a-pawns block each other and each king runs for the other's pawn: the white one has already gone to e6 and the black one to c3. Schlage has two roads to c6: via d6 or via d5. One wins and the other draws. Which, and why?
step.t_schlage.hint1: Where does the black king want to go? Trace its path to c7: it needs to get there before your king takes a7 and leaves the corner.
step.t_schlage.hint2: Count both kings' moves along the two roads. On which one does the black king lose a tempo getting to c7?
step.schlage: Schlage played 2.Kd6? and Ahues answered 2...Kd4! The black king came in through the square White had left open. After 3.Kc6 Ke5 4.Kb7 Kd6 5.Kxa7 Kc7 the black king reached c7, the white one was locked in the corner in front of its own pawn, and the game ended in a draw. The right move was 2.Kd5! The white king passes through the square that shuts d4: the black king has to go around via b4, and that tempo is the win. This is shouldering in a master game, and it is the game the books use to teach the technique.
step.d_schlageDraw: See what happened in the game, with the white king on d6.
step.d_schlageDraw.m1: 2...Kd4! The black king comes in through the open square and runs for c7.
step.d_schlageDraw.m2: 3.Kc6. Schlage heads for b7, to take a7.
step.d_schlageDraw.m3: 3...Ke5. Ahues advances along the diagonal, at the same speed.
step.d_schlageDraw.m5: 4...Kd6. After 5.Kxa7 Kc7 the white king is on a7, locked in front of its own pawn: Schlage and Ahues drew.
step.d_schlageWin: Now the win, as the books showed after the game.
step.d_schlageWin.m1: 2.Kd5! I shut d4: the black king does not come in through the middle.
step.d_schlageWin.m2: 2...Kb4. It has to go around the outside.
step.d_schlageWin.m3: 3.Kc6. I shut b5 and c5; it stays behind me.
step.d_schlageWin.m4: 3...Ka5. It waits beside the pawn: there is no better square.
step.d_schlageWin.m6: 4...Kb5. It runs for c6, but arrives a tempo late.
step.d_schlageWin.m7: 5.Kxa7. Pawn taken; now my king has to get out from in front of the pawn before the black king shuts c7.
step.d_schlageWin.m8: 5...Kc6. It wants c7, to lock me in the corner as in the game.
step.d_schlageWin.m9: 6.Kb8! I get out one move before it shuts the door: 6...Kb6 7.a7 and the pawn queens.
step.schlageMove: Now you are Schlage, with the chance he missed: take the king to c6 through the right square and capture a7.
step.schlageMove.hint: The square that shuts d4 to the black king.
step.schlageMove.done: Yes. 2.Kd5! was the win, and you found it. Schlage played 2.Kd6? and drew.
step.t_away: The plan is to take the f7-pawn without losing your own. 1.Kf5 looks like the natural road. Does it work?
step.t_away.hint1: After 1.Kf5, where does the black king go? Is your f3-pawn left on its own?
step.t_away.hint2: The black king wants to reach f3 via g2. Before going up, shut that door.
step.away: 1.Kf5? Kg2 2.f4 Kf3 and the black king reaches my pawn: draw. The right move is 1.Kg3! It steps away from f7, but it shuts g2 and f2, and the black king is locked on the first rank. Meanwhile the pawn goes up under cover. When it reaches f6, my king takes f7 and, at the same time, defends its own pawn.
step.d_away: Two shoulders in a row: one to hold the black king down, another to push it aside.
step.d_away.m1: 1.Kg3. I shut g2 and f2: the black king does not come up on the kingside.
step.d_away.m2: 1...Kg1. It looks for another door: f1 and then e2.
step.d_away.m3: 2.f4. The pawn advances while my king looks after it; every pawn move is a tempo the black king loses.
step.d_away.m4: 2...Kf1. It will go around through the centre, via e2.
step.d_away.m5: 3.f5. One more step: from f6 the pawn will support the capture of f7.
step.d_away.m6: 3...Ke2. The black king finally comes up, through the middle.
step.d_away.m7: 4.Kf4! The second shoulder: e3 and e4 are shut, and it has to go around. After 4...Kd3 5.Ke5 Ke3 6.f6, the f7-pawn falls with mine protected.
step.awayMove: Repeat the plan: first lock the black king down below, then the second shoulder.
step.awayMove.hint: The first move steps the king away from the f7-pawn and shuts g2.
step.awayMove.done: Yes. 1.Kg3 and then 4.Kf4: the black king never got near the white pawn.
step.d_later: Now the capture that waits. The b7-pawn is within reach: 1.Kc5? and 2.Kb6 would take it. But 1...Ke5! 2.Kb6 Kd4 3.Kxb7 Kc4 4.b4 Kxb4 is a draw: the black king reached my pawn. First its path, then the pawn.
step.d_later.m1: 1.Kd5! I shut e5 and e6: the black king does not come in.
step.d_later.m2: 1...Kf6. It tries e7, the only passage left towards my pawn.
step.d_later.m4: 2...Kf7. It will go around via e8.
step.d_later.m5: 3.b4. Now the pawn: the black king is four files away and the way around is long.
step.d_later.m6: 3...Ke8. Too late: the black king went all the way around and the pawn is already on b4.
step.d_later.m7: 4.Kc7! The b7-pawn falls further up: 4...b5 5.Kc6 and I take it on b5 with my king in front of my own pawn.
step.laterMove: The b7-pawn is within reach, but first shut the black king's path.
step.laterMove.hint: Before going for the pawn, shut e5 and e6: that is the black king's way to your pawn.
step.laterMove.done: Yes. 1.Kd5 and 2.Kd6 shut the e-file; the b7-pawn falls later, and closer to my king.
step.t_square: The g6-pawn wants to run, and the black king wants to reach my f2-pawn. One king move does both: it stays in the square of the black pawn and shuts the path of the black king. Which?
step.t_square.hint1: Mark the square of the g6-pawn: from g6 to g1 and from b6 to b1. From which squares does your king stay inside it?
step.t_square.hint2: Inside the square, which square takes c4 and c5 away from the black king?
step.square: 1.Kd4! I stay in the square of the g6-pawn and shut c4 and c5 at the same time. 1.Ke5?, which looks like running for the pawn, allows 1...Kc4! and the black king reaches my pawn: 2.Kf6 Kd3 3.Kxg6 Ke4, draw. After 1...Kc6 2.Ke5! again does both things: it stays in the square and shuts d5 and d6. This is the idea of the studies by Duras and by Grigoriev that you will meet in the exercises.
step.d_square: One move, two jobs, twice in a row.
step.d_square.m1: 1.Kd4! In the square of g6 and shutting c4 and c5.
step.d_square.m2: 1...Kc6. It tries d5 along the sixth rank.
step.d_square.m3: 2.Ke5! Both things again: in the square of the g6-pawn, with d5 and d6 shut.
step.d_square.m4: 2...g5. With no road for the king, the pawn runs.
step.d_square.m5: 3.Kf5. I stay in the new square, from g5 to c1, and shut e4 and e6.
step.d_square.m7: 4.Kxg4. Pawn taken, and the black king far from my f-pawn: king and pawn against king, a win.
step.squareMove: Stay in the square of the g-pawn and, with the same move, shut the black king's path.
step.squareMove.hint: Stay in the square of the g-pawn and shut the square the black king would come in through.
step.squareMove.done: Yes. 1.Kd4 and 2.Ke5: one move, two jobs. That is how Duras and Grigoriev win in the exercises.
step.raceMove: Now in a race: the black king is going to take f5 and come back to stop my a-pawn. Put your king in the way of that return.
step.raceMove.hint: The king heads for c6, where it shuts d6 and d7, the squares the black king wants to come back through.
step.raceMove.done: Well done. With the king on c6, Black cannot stop the a-pawn. After 3...f5 4.a5 f4 5.a6 f3 6.a7 f2 7.a8=Q f1=Q both queens are born, but 8.Qe8+ Kf5 9.Qf8+ skewers the queen on f1.
step.recap: Three rules. One: before running for a pawn, look where the other king wants to go and stand in its path; on the stairs, my king goes on the black king's file, two ranks below, and Schlage would have won with 2.Kd5! Two: the wall moves along, on the black king's rank, two files away, all the way to the edge of the board. Three: the right move does not always head straight for the target: it may step away from it, like 1.Kg3!, put off the capture, like 1.Kd5!, or do two things at once, like 1.Kd4!, which stays in the square and shuts the path.
step.defend: The defender uses the same shoulder. This is a study by Grigoriev, from 1925: 1.Kf6? looks natural, but 1...Kg4! 2.Kxf7 Kf5! and it is the black king that shoulders: 3.Ke7 Ke5 4.Kd7 Kd5 5.Kc7 Kc5, and the b5-pawn falls. That is why 1.Kf5! shuts the g-file; the black king is locked on the h-file, I go down with it, and the b5-pawn is never in danger.
step.d_defendPunish: See the punishment with the white king on f6. The board turns: now you watch from Black's side, as Black uses the shoulder against White.
step.d_defendPunish.m1: 1...Kg4! Instead of defending f7, the black king goes for White's b5-pawn.
step.d_defendPunish.m2: 2.Kxf7. White wins a pawn, but the king ends up on the wrong side.
step.d_defendPunish.m3: 2...Kf5! The shoulder against White: e6 and e5 are shut, and the white king does not get back through the middle.
step.d_defendPunish.m4: 3.Ke7. The white king tries to get back over the top, along the seventh rank, but the black king moves along with it.
step.d_defendPunish.m6: 4.Kd7. Closer to the pawn, but always behind.
step.d_defendPunish.m7: 4...Kd5. And after 5.Kc7 Kc5 6.Kb7 Kxb5 the pawn falls: Black wins.
step.defendMove: Lock the black king on the h-file and go down with it.
step.defendMove.hint: Your king stays on the f-file, on the same rank as the black king.
step.defendMove.done: Yes. 1.Kf5, 2.Kf4, 3.Kf3 and 4.Kf2: the black king was locked on the edge, and your b5-pawn was never in danger.
step.finish: First the shoulder, then the pawn. I defend with Black.
ex.e02: The black king is in the corner. How does your king keep it there while the e-pawn runs? Find the winning move.
ex.e02.hint: The black king would leave the corner via g8 and f8. One square shuts both.
ex.e02.solution: 1.Kf7! shuts g8 and the black king's way back to the centre. It stays between h8, h7 and h6, and the e-pawn runs with nobody to stop it.
ex.e05: Your king wants to go and take the a4-pawn. 1.Kf5 looks like the shortest way. Is it the best? Find the winning move.
ex.e05.hint: The black king will run to c8, the good corner against a rook's pawn. Shut its road along the seventh rank.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Kf6! (the only move) takes g7, f7 and e7 away from the black king. It has to go around along the eighth rank, and the white king reaches b6 first. With 1.Kf5? the black king goes down via g7, f7, e7, reaches c8 and draws.
ex.e08: The plan is to take b7. 1.Kc4 looks like the direct road. What is the right first move? Find the winning move.
ex.e08.hint: Before heading for b7, keep the black king away from your a-pawn. It comes via f2 and e3.
ex.e08.solution: 1.Ke2! (the only move) shuts f1, f2 and f3; then 2.a4 and 3.Ke3, also the only moves. The black king stays behind the white one all the way, and the white king reaches b7 without being caught. With 1.Kc4? the black king comes via f2, e3, d4 and c4 and arrives in time.
ex.e10: Study by Grigoriev, 1932. White to move and win. The c7-pawn is about to run, and the black king wants to step into the square of your a-pawn. One move handles both.
ex.e10.hint: The black king heads for the queenside along the fourth rank. Shut that road and go for the c-pawn at the same time.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Kf5!, 2.Ke5! and 3.Kd4!, all the only moves. The white king goes for the c-pawn and, at every step, shuts e4 and d4 to the black king. With 1.a4? comes 1...Ke4, and the black king is inside the pawn's square. In the end the white king takes the c-pawn and the black king arrives too late for the a-pawn.
ex.e11: Study by Duras, 1905. White to move and win. Your king has to stop the g-pawn and, at the same time, see the b-pawn home. Only one move does both.
ex.e11.hint: The black king will come back through the centre to catch your pawn. Put your king where it shuts that road without leaving the square of the g-pawn.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Kc5! (the only move). The king stays inside the square of the g-pawn and already shuts d6 and d7 to the black king. After 1...Kg6, 2.b4, 2...Kf7, 3.b5, 3...Ke7 comes 4.Kc6, and the black king never gets in front of the pawn. With 1.Kc4? Kg5 the black king returns via f6 and e7 in time; 1.b3? only draws as well.
ex.e12: In a plain race both sides queen, and a c-pawn on the seventh with its king beside it draws against the queen. You need another plan. Find the winning move.
ex.e12.hint: Before pushing the h-pawn, use your king to keep the black king out of that pawn's square, without blocking the diagonal of your future queen.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Ke4! and 2.Kd4!, both the only moves: the white king threatens the c-pawn and shoulders the black king away from the square of the h-pawn. 2.Ke5? blocks the h8-b2 diagonal and draws; 1.h4? at once is the race that draws. After 2...Kb4 comes 3.h4 and, against 3...c5+, 4.Ke3! (the only move), not d3, where it would take another check. At the end the king on d2 watches c1: if the pawn queens, the king takes it; if the black king goes to b2, the promotion on h8 comes with check.
ex.e13: Study by Mandler, 1938. White to move and win. Taking b7 or racing with the f-pawn look natural. Calculate first.
ex.e13.hint: The right move takes nothing and pushes nothing: it hands Black the first move in the race, but leaves your king on the road the black king needs.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kd6!! (the only move). If the b-pawn advances, the white king takes it further up and stands between the black king and the f-pawn. So 1...Ka3, and 2.Kc5! (the only move) stays in the way; the black king has to walk up the a-file to escort its pawn, and only then 3.f4! (the only move) and the race belongs to White. With 1.f4? b5 both sides queen and it's a draw; with 1.Kxb7? Kb3 the black king catches the f-pawn; with 1.Kb6? Kb3 it steps into the square.
key.stairs: The white king walks down beside the black one, like going down stairs, always taking the square it wanted, until it is left far from the pawn.
key.wall: The white king becomes a wall in the middle of the board: the black king cannot get across to the pawns.
key.across: Shouldering from one side of the board to the other: the white king keeps walking down between the black king and the far side, and never lets it cross.
key.away: Before going for the pawns, the white king takes one step sideways and blocks the black king's path, leaving it stranded far from everything.
key.race: Shouldering in a race: the white king advances and, with the same moves, keeps the black king out of the path of White's edge pawn.
key.defend: Shouldering also saves games: the white king stands in the black king's path and stops it helping its pawn. The exact square matters: one to the side, and you lose.
key.corner: The black king is in the corner with only two ways out. The white king takes the square that shuts both, and the pawn runs all the way with no need for an escort.
key.schlage: Berlin, 1921: Willi Schlage, with White, against Carl Ahues. Both kings were running for the other side's pawn, and Schlage chose the road that looked most direct. Ahues slipped through the middle, locked the white king in the corner and snatched the draw. Through the square next door, Schlage would have won: it is the game the books use to teach shouldering.
key.later: The black pawn is within reach, but whoever takes it at once leaves his own king out of the way and draws. The white king first shuts the black king's passage; the pawn falls later, and closer to the white pawn.
key.square: A king move that does two things: it stays inside the square of the black pawn, to catch it if it runs, and at the same time blocks the black king's road to the white pawn.
history: Shouldering means using your own king as a barrier: it stands in the enemy king's path and pushes it away without touching it, like a defender stepping into an attacker's path. It is one of the classic named ideas of pawn endings; Mark Dvoretsky gives it a section in his endgame manual, next to opposition and triangulation. It looks simple but it is very deceptive: several published studies and handouts give the wrong route, because a single square to one side is enough to turn a win into a loss. You have already met shouldering in passing in other lessons; here it is the main subject.
practice: Now the practical challenge: king and pawn against king, from start to finish. Before you move the pawn, put your king in the black king's way.
